name: nwchem
why: Real high-performance computational chemistry you can run at home, though it is serious research software with a steep curve.

brief.what_it_is: NWChem is an open-source computational chemistry package that its maintainers describe as tools for tackling complex scientific problems. The homepage says it covers biomolecules, nanostructures and solid-state systems, quantum and classical methods and combinations of them, ground and excited states, Gaussian basis functions or plane waves, and properties and relativistic effects. The pages I read do not spell out the exact input or output file format. They do mention 'input decks' and 'output decks', and the EMSL Arrows service helps generate input decks and check output decks against a large database of calculations. The installed command is nwchem.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the software was developed to use the aggregate resources of supercomputers and computer clusters efficiently. The development strategy targets kinetics and dynamics of chemical transformations, chemistry at interfaces and in the condensed phase, and integrated research at EMSL, plus scaling to architectures of tens of petaflops and beyond.
brief.how_it_works: The pages I read do not explain the internal mechanism. They do say it scales from one to thousands of processors and uses Gaussian basis functions or plane waves. The EMSL Arrows web API is a separate front end aimed at beginners for generating input decks, checking outputs, doing simple thermochemistry, and computing NMR and IR spectra for modest-sized molecules.

brief.install_notes: The README offers source only, not a build guide. You can git clone the master branch or the release-7-3-0 hotfix branch. Release 7.3.1 comes as two tarballs, a source-only one and a non-source-only one, both dated 2025-11-06 in their filenames. Release notes are in release.notes.7.3.1.md in the repo. Homebrew installs the nwchem executable (brew install nwchem). The README badges also show Conda-Forge and Docker Pulls (nwchemorg/nwchem-700.fedora.sockets), which suggests those are alternative install routes, though I did not verify the instructions for them. The pages I read give no hardware, account, runtime or first-run configuration details, and the documentation link on the homepage was not followed for build steps.
brief.standout: Beyond the solver, NWChem's maintainers run EMSL Arrows, a web service for newcomers that generates input decks, checks output decks against a large calculation database, does simple thermochemistry, and computes NMR and IR spectra, so you can try it before installing. It is also built to scale from a laptop-sized problem to thousands of processors.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage names 7.3.1 as the latest release. The release tarballs are dated 2025-11-06. The README has CI badges, a release notes file and active EMSL and PNNL maintenance. I did not check the commit log, so the date of the latest commit is unknown.
brief.caveats: The pages I read give no build or run instructions, so install effort is unclear beyond Homebrew and the source tarballs. The homepage describes it as serious research software aimed at supercomputers and research users, which means a steep learning curve. The distribution is under the Educational Community License 2.0 (ECL 2.0). The EMSL Arrows API is described as in alpha testing. Scout notes say it is runnable at home, but the pages I read do not confirm that for a laptop.

entry.title: NWChem
entry.tldr: An open-source computational chemistry package from a US national lab, built to run quantum and classical molecular simulations from one processor up to thousands.
entry.deeper_look:
NWChem is a computational chemistry package maintained by the Environmental Molecular Sciences Laboratory (EMSL) at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory in Washington State. Its homepage lists a wide scope: biomolecules, nanostructures and solid-state systems, quantum and classical methods and combinations of them, ground and excited states, Gaussian basis functions or plane waves, and properties and relativistic effects.

It exists to make good use of big machines. The homepage says the software was developed "to efficiently use the aggregate resources available on supercomputers or computer clusters", and the project's stated strategy targets chemical kinetics and dynamics, chemistry at interfaces and in the condensed phase, and scaling to architectures of tens of petaflops and beyond. It scales "from one to thousands of processors", so a small job on a single machine is within its design range.

The idea underneath is that you describe a molecule and a calculation in an input file, which the project calls an input deck, and the program works out the physics and writes an output deck. The pages read for this entry do not spell out the file format, so the documentation is the place to learn it. The maintainers also run EMSL Arrows, a web service for newcomers that helps generate input decks, checks output decks against a large database of calculations, and does simple thermochemistry plus NMR and IR spectra for modest-sized molecules. It is a way to see what the field's inputs and outputs look like before installing anything.
entry.install:
brew install nwchem
# Installs the nwchem executable. The formula pulls in gcc, open-mpi, openblas, scalapack, libxc and python. Source tarballs for release 7.3.1 are on the GitHub releases page.

try_this.what_happens: Runs the installed executable with a help flag. The brief did not confirm what it prints, so check the documentation if it does not behave like a usual help screen.
Clones the master branch of the source repository, so you can read the code and the release notes.
Clones the 7.3.1 release line into a directory named nwchem-7.3.1.

entry.whats_unique: It is serious research-grade chemistry software from a national lab, designed to scale to supercomputers, with a web front end (EMSL Arrows) that lets beginners try input and output decks without installing it.
entry.caveats: This is research software with a steep learning curve, the pages read gave no run instructions, and the EMSL Arrows API is described as in alpha testing.
